paragraphs.text: (1) The appellant may discontinue the appeal by filing and serving a notice to discontinue in Form AP-4, and the respondent is entitled to a costs award for having responded to the appeal. (2) The discontinuance of an appeal does not operate as a discontinuance of a cross appeal. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4

paragraphs.text: (1) A single appeal judge may order a party to provide security for payment of a costs award pursuant to Part 4, Division 4. (2) Where a party does not provide security as ordered, the appeal is deemed to have been abandoned and the other party is entitled to a costs award. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4

Arres Capital Inc., 2017 ABCA 373, 2017 CarswellAlta 2397, 63 Alta. L.R. (6th) 217, Justice Rowbotham gave this overview, and comment on the differences between R. 14.67 and previous Rule 524: 3 Rule 14.67 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 (Rules of Court) sets out the ability of this court to order that a party provide security for costs … 4 Part 4, Division 4 of the Rules of Court includes Rule 4.22 which sets out the factors that a court must consider when evaluating an application for a security for costs order under Rule 14.67 …. 5 The onus is on the applicant to prove these factors weigh in its favour: Aski Construction Ltd v Markos, 2017 ABCA 341 at para 8, 2017 CarswellAlta 1845. 6 The test for security for costs from Rules 4.22 and 14.67 of the Rules of Court differs from the earlier requirements of now repealed Rule 524 of the previous Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/1968 (“Old Rules”) which read (emphasis added): 524. (1) No security for costs shall be required in appeals unless by reason of special circumstances security is ordered by a judge. (2) Unless the court otherwise orders an appellant who fails to give security for costs when ordered shall be deemed to have abandoned his appeal and the respondent is entitled to his costs. 7 During the course of the application, an issue arose as to whether “special circumstances” were required before this court could order security for costs on appeal. 8 For the sake of clarity, Rule 524 of the Old Rules, as it applied to this court, was repealed by Alberta Rules of Court Amendment Regulation 2014, Alta Reg 41/2014, s 4, which came into force September 1, 2014. Its replacement includes Rule 14.67 of the Rules of Court. Rule 14.67 does not refer to “special circumstances”, instead referencing the factors in Rule 4.22. Accordingly, it would seem that pre-September 2014 decisions of this court that reference tests involving special circumstances in the context of security for costs, have effectively been overtaken by Rules of Court. 9 The commentary in the Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2018 (Stevenson & Côté (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2018)) notes that “[t]he former stiff test (in old R. 524) is gone, and the lax test in R. 4.22 now applies. So most pre-2014 case law on the tests for security in the Court of Appeal probably does not apply”: 14–143. 10 This position is supported by recent decisions of this court that do not refer to special circumstances: see e.g. Stacey v Foy, 2014 ABCA 420, 247 ACWS (3d) 789 (single judge); Haymour v Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367, 273 ACWS (3d) 47 (panel); and Aski Construction Ltd (single judge). 11 Nevertheless, given that Rule 4.22(e) enables the court to consider “any other matter” it considers appropriate, if a party thought that there were special circumstances, they might be considered under the catchall Rule 4.22(e). In Aubin v. Condominium Plan No. 862 2917, 2024 ABCA 201, Justice Feehan provided this summary of the law: [6] The test for granting security for costs is set out in Poole v City Wide Towing and Recovery Service Ltd, 2020 ABCA 102, paras 47-50; Milot Law v Sittler, 2024 ABCA 116, para 15; PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc v Perpetual Energy Inc, 2020 ABCA 36, para 15, 18, 20, 75 CBR (6th) 179; Haymour v The Owners Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367, para 8. The applicant bears the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that it is just and equitable to order security for costs or that the respondent will be unable to pay costs that may be awarded. [7] This Court said in Parker v. Parker, 2019 ABCA 114, para 4, 89 Alta LR (6th) 104: A security for costs order is discretionary and balances the reasonable expectations of the parties with their rights in order to arrive at a just and reasonable outcome: Haymour … at para 8. The onus rests with the applicant to establish that the factors in r 4.22 are met: Aski Construction Ltd v Markos, 2017 ABCA 341 at para 8. A failure to pay costs awarded in previous trial court processes, along with a demonstrated inability to pay costs if an appeal is unsuccessful, will be sufficient to grant a security for costs order in most cases: DataNet Information Systems, Inc v Belzil, 2011 ABCA 40 (chambers) at para 4. “Access to justice does not equate to access to civil processes without fear of costs consequences”: ibid. See also: Stoney v Trustees for the 1985 Sawridge Trust, 2017 ABCA 437, para 6. [8] Concerns regarding a party’s ability to pay costs coupled with modest prospects of an appeal’s success have been sufficient to justify granting an application for security for costs: Skolney v Nisha, 2018 ABCA 78, para 15, 10 RFL (8th) 34. [9] Granting security for costs is discretionary and requires the court to look to the equities of the case before making an order. The court may make an order if it “considers it just and reasonable to do so”, taking into consideration the elements set out in rule 4.22: Skolney, para 21. 2. Reasonable Chance of Success at Appeal Where an appellant has a reasonable prospect of success, he should not be prevented from appealing because he cannot secure the costs of his opponents. Locke v. Calgary (City) (1994), 162 A.R. 188 (C.A.), at 189, per Hetherington J.A. 3. Trial Costs That leads to the question of how much the security should be. Counsel for the defendant/respondent suggested the full amount of the trial costs unpaid, plus the likely amount of costs of the appeal. But despite the authorities which he cited, notably Fabing v. Conceicao (1986), 54 O.R. 402 at 406 (C.A.), it seems to me there should not be security for the trial costs. There may be situations where that would be appropriate. For example, where R. 593 applies and the defendant might get security for the trial costs, and there is also some reason for applying late. Or maybe a case where it is the appellant's fault which has taken assets from the respondent, so that the respondent would now lack funds to fight the appeal. It might also be different if the appellant seemed to be acting in bad faith, the litigation were particularly vexatious, or the appellant were seeking some other special relief such as a late appeal or a stay of execution. Verth v. Howrie (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 441 (C.A.), at 442–43, per Côté J.A. In Poole v. City Wide Towing and Recovery Service Ltd, 2020 ABCA 102, 2020 CarswellAlta 440, 62 C.C.E.L. (4th) 184, Justice Feehan gave this summary of the test of security for costs: [47] The applicant bears the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that it is just and equitable to order security for costs or that the respondent will be unable to pay costs that may be awarded: PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc v Perpetual Energy Inc., 2020 ABCA 36, para 18. This is a disjunctive test. [48] The test is succinctly summarized in Parker v Parker, 2019 ABCA 114, para 4, 89 Alta LR (6th) 104: A security for costs order is discretionary and balances the reasonable expectations of the parties with their rights in order to arrive at a just and reasonable outcome: Haymour v The Owners Condominium Plan No 802 2845, 2016 ABCA 367 at para 8. The onus rests with the applicant to establish that the factors in r 4.22 are met: Aski Construction Ltd v Markos, 2017 ABCA 341 at para 8. A failure to pay costs awarded in previous trial court processes, along with a demonstrated inability to pay costs if an appeal is unsuccessful, will be sufficient to grant a security for costs order in most cases: DataNet Information Systems, Inc v Belzil, 2011 ABCA 40 (chambers) at para 4. “Access to justice does not equate to access to civil processes without fear of costs consequences”: ibid. [49] In Skolney v Nisha, 2018 ABCA 78, para 15, 10 RFL (8th) 34, this Court said: Concerns regarding a party's ability to pay costs coupled with modest prospects of an appeal's success have been sufficient to justify granting an application for security for costs: see for example Matty v Rammasoot, 2013 ABCA 170, [2013] AWLD 3062. [50] The granting of security for costs is discretionary and requires the chambers judge to look to the equities of the case before making an order. The court may make an order if it “considers it just and reasonable to do so”, taking into consideration the elements set out in rule 4.22 (Skolney, para 21). O'Leary J.A. has said: The authorities indicate that ordering an appellant to post security for all or part of unpaid trial costs is not that common in this Province. The wording of rule 524(1) is no doubt the source of the reluctance to require security for unpaid trial costs as a condition of prosecuting an appeal. It is not unusual for the costs taxed against an appellant at trial to remain unpaid in whole or in part. They may exceed the security posted at trial, if any security was ordered at that level. An unsuccessful party at trial may become impecunious or otherwise unable to pay the costs taxed against him or her at trial. Sometimes that is caused by the actions of the respondent. An appellate court cannot be seen as an agency to ensure collection of trial costs. Sorrel 1985 Ltd. Partnership v. Sorrel Resources Ltd. (1998), 219 A.R. 2 at 5 (C.A.). In Skolney v. Nisha, 2018 ABCA 78, 2018 CarswellAlta 342, 10 R.F.L. (8th) 34, Justice Greckol said: [12] The Court of Appeal does not normally grant security for the payment of trial costs because it is not an “agency to ensure the collection of trial costs”: 1159465 Alberta Ltd v Adwood Manufacturing Ltd, 2010 ABCA 273 (CanLII) at para 10, 35 Alta LR (5th) 37, quoting Pivotal Capital Advisory Group Ltd v NorAmera BioEnergy Corporation, 2008 ABCA 279 (CanLII) at para 10, [2008] AJ No 844 (QL). Insofar as Mr. Skolney seeks payment as a condition of Ms. Nisha's appeal proceeding further, there is no statutory authority to make such an order or to strike an appeal if Ms. Nisha does not comply. 4. Unpaid Trial Costs In Freyberg v. Fletcher Challenge Oil and Gas Inc. (2003), 330 A.R. 130 (C.A.), Conrad J.A. said, at pp. 134-135: Finally, I wish to comment briefly on conflicting comments as to the impact of unpaid trial costs on an application for security. Justice Wittmann, in Ellis, relying on Verth v. Howrie (1995), 169 A.R. 398, 97 W.A.C. 398, 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 441 (C.A.), stated that security for trial costs can be ordered where it could have been obtained or where it is the appellant's fault that assets are not available to the respondent. However, Ellis must be considered having regard to the findings and reasoning of the underlying precedent: Verth, supra. In Verth (at para. 5) Justice Côté stated “it seems to me that there should not be security for trial costs.” Justice Côté then went on to acknowledge that there may be cases where security for trial costs could be awarded: such as where there is a persuasive reason for the late application of rule 593, the appellant's actions deprive the respondent of the assets to fight the appeal, the existence of bad faith, particularly vexatious litigation, or an appellant seeks some special relief such as a late appeal or stay of execution. Verth did not suggest that costs would be ordered at the appellate level simply because they could have been obtained at the trial level. Justice Wittmann's comments were made in reliance of Verth, and his decision was made on the specific circumstances of the case before him. In my view, if trial costs could have been obtained at the trial level, they should have been sought at that level, and the fact that they are unpaid by the time of the appeal should ot support the application for security. Security for costs is a remedy to secure that portion of a proceeding that has yet to take place. To hold otherwise is to change the rules after the fact. While Verth notes some circumstances where an order of trial costs is just and equitable, the order is the exception and not the rule. While unpaid trial costs may be some evidence of future anticipated difficulty in collecting costs, it is just a factor to consider and if there are sufficient assets to pay appellate costs alone, that should suffice. Difficulty of collection alone is not a special circumstance. An order for security upon appeal should not be used to indirectly result in securing trial costs. As Justice O'Leary held in Sorrel 1985 Limited Partnership et al. v. Sorrel Resources Ltd. et al. (1998), 219 A.R. 2, 179 W.A.C. 2 (C.A.), at para. 13, “[a]n appellate court cannot be seen as an agency to ensure collection of trial costs”. 5. Security for Judgment In Vaillancourt v. Carter, 2017 ABCA 282, Justice O'Ferrall had before him an application by the respondent in the appeal for an order compelling the appellant to post security for judgment before being permitted to prosecute the appeal. His Lordship said at paragraphs 20–25: 20 Security for judgment is an extraordinary remedy that can only be granted in exceptional circumstances (Aetna Financial Services Ltd v Feigelman, [1985] 1 SCR 2 at 10, 15 DLR (4th) 161; CH v MH, 1997 ABCA 263 at para 24, (sub nom Hamza v Hamza) 53 Alta LR (3d) 80. An order for security for judgment requires that the appellant post the required security before continuing with his or her appeal. In this way, security for judgment functions much like a mareva injunction and restrains the appellant from disposing of or dissipating a portion of his assets in order that they be available to satisfy the judgment should it be upheld (Vaccaro v Twin Cities Power-Canada ULC, 2013 ABCA 252 at para 14, 97 Alta LR (5th) 193). If security for judgment is ordered and not posted, the appeal is dismissed. 21 Historically, courts have been reluctant to grant security for judgment, holding that such an exceptional remedy may preclude appellants with a lack of financial resources from pursuing their appeals (Carr v Bower Cotton (A Firm), [2002] EWCA Civ 789 (BAILII) at para 33; Creative Salmon Co v Staniford, 2007 BCCA 285 at para 12, 242 BCAC 299). That does not appear to be the case here. But, as well, courts have held that recovery of judgment is more appropriately dealt with through enforcement proceedings (Barclay-Johnson v Yuill, [1980] 1 WLR 1259 at 1262-63, [1980] 3 All ER 190; Aikenhead v Jenkins, 2002 BCCA 234 at para 31, 166 BCAC 293). Jurisprudence which favours enforcement proceedings over applications for security for judgments is of particular relevance, given that an appeal does not operate as a stay of enforcement in Alberta. Successful plaintiffs remain free to enforce their judgments (Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, s 14.68). 22 Enforcement proceedings are the prescribed and preferred way that judgments are enforced. The Civil Enforcement Act not only provides for an exhaustive code of writs of enforcement (Wagner v Wagner, 2014 ABCA 428 at para 44, 588 AR 218), but it also provides protections for both creditors and debtors which cannot be easily replicated by courts in granting security for judgments (Direct Norkus (Estate of) v Direct Rental Centre (West) Ltd, 2001 ABCA 233 at para 25, 205 DLR (4th) 651). By way of example, I note that under s. 2(d) of the Civil Enforcement Act, enforcement proceedings taken by one execution creditor are taken on behalf of all execution creditors of the debtor. This protection precludes a single enforcement creditor receiving a preference over other creditors, which can happen if security for judgment orders become commonplace or are not made subject to conditions. 23 The comprehensive scheme of enforcement provided by the Civil Enforcement Act suggests that the Court of Appeal should rarely make orders which interfere with statutorily-prescribed enforcement processes (Guarantee RV Centre Inc v Schmidt, 2007 ABCA 193 at para 7, 412 AR 21). Litigants cannot view this court as an agency for the collection of trial costs or as a way to circumvent the ordinary enforcement process (Sorrel 1985 Ltd Partnership v Sorrel Resources Ltd, 1998 ABCA 103 at para 13, 219 AR 2). To do so would be an abuse of process. An application for security for judgment is therefore warranted only in the most extreme cases and, as a general rule, will not be granted. 24 However, in some circumstances, an order for security for judgment may be justified. There are a few notable exceptions to the general rule against granting security for judgment. From canvassing the case law, I find that an order preserving the assets of one party is available: 1. where there are no assets in the jurisdiction against which to enforce a judgment and the appeal has little merit (Vaccaro at para 11; Creative Salmon at para 12; Richland Construction Inc v Manningwa Developments Inc., 1996 CarswellBC 1767 (WL Can) at paras 12-13 (CA)); 2. to preserve assets that would otherwise be destroyed, disposed of, or dissipated prior to the resolution of the dispute (Hamza at paras 26–30; 1400467 Alberta Ltd v Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439 at para 52, 591 AR 40; Vaccaro at para 15; Aetna Financial at 12); and 3. to encourage respect for the judicial process and avoid abuse of process (Hamza at para 23, citing Mooney v Orr (1994), 100 BCLR (2d) 335 at 348 (BCSC) [Mooney cited in this judgment to 1994 CarswellBC 26 (WL Can)]; Vaccaro at paras 12–14; Aetna Financial at 12). 25 The exception that I am most concerned with in this application is encouraging respect for the judicial process and avoiding abuse of process and, to a lesser extent, avoiding the disposition of assets prior to ultimate resolution. As Huddart J. stated in Mooney at paragraphs 66–69: • A litigant cannot be permitted to use the court to his advantage while effectively disavowing in advance any judgment against him … (the ordering of the security is) not to enhance the claimant's rights, but to ensure that those reasonable people who pay for the administration of justice in this province are not affronted by the impotence of the court in the face of those who choose to order their affairs so as to keep all their options for themselves. 6. Rule is Constitutional In Trisura Guarantee Insurance v. Duchnij, et al., 2021 ABCA 78, 2021 CarswellAlta 461, 26 Alta. L.R. (7th) 1, 13 C.C.L.I. (6th) 6, Justice Wakeling said, at paragraph 10: [10] Rule 14.67 of the Alberta Rules of Court is not inconsistent with the Constitution Act, 1867. …

If security for judgment is ordered and not posted, the appeal is dismissed.

21 Historically, courts have been reluctant to grant security for judgment, holding that such an exceptional remedy may preclude appellants with a lack of financial resources from pursuing their appeals (Carr v Bower Cotton (A Firm), [2002] EWCA Civ 789 (BAILII) at para 33
Creative Salmon Co v Staniford, 2007 BCCA 285 at para 12, 242 BCAC 299).
That does not appear to be the case here.
But, as well, courts have held that recovery of judgment is more appropriately dealt with through enforcement proceedings (Barclay-Johnson v Yuill, [1980] 1 WLR 1259 at 1262-63, [1980] 3 All ER 190
Aikenhead v Jenkins, 2002 BCCA 234 at para 31, 166 BCAC 293).
Jurisprudence which favours enforcement proceedings over applications for security for judgments is of particular relevance, given that an appeal does not operate as a stay of enforcement in Alberta.
Successful plaintiffs remain free to enforce their judgments (Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010, s 14.68).
22 Enforcement proceedings are the prescribed and preferred way that judgments are enforced.

The Civil Enforcement Act not only provides for an exhaustive code of writs of enforcement (Wagner v Wagner, 2014 ABCA 428 at para 44, 588 AR 218), but it also provides protections for both creditors and debtors which cannot be easily replicated by courts in granting security for judgments (Direct Norkus (Estate of) v Direct Rental Centre (West) Ltd, 2001 ABCA 233 at para 25, 205 DLR
By way of example, I note that under s.
2(d) of the Civil Enforcement Act, enforcement proceedings taken by one execution creditor are taken on behalf of all execution creditors of the debtor.

This protection precludes a single enforcement creditor receiving a preference over other creditors, which can happen if security for judgment orders become commonplace or are not made subject to conditions.

23 The comprehensive scheme of enforcement provided by the Civil Enforcement Act suggests that the Court of Appeal should rarely make orders which interfere with statutorily-prescribed enforcement processes (Guarantee RV Centre Inc v Schmidt, 2007 ABCA 193 at para 7, 412 AR 21).

Litigants cannot view this court as an agency for the collection of trial costs or as a way to circumvent the ordinary enforcement process (Sorrel 1985 Ltd Partnership v Sorrel Resources Ltd, 1998 ABCA 103 at para 13, 219 AR 2).
To do so would be an abuse of process.
An application for security for judgment is therefore warranted only in the most extreme cases and, as a general rule, will not be granted.
24 However, in some circumstances, an order for security for judgment may be justified.
There are a few notable exceptions to the general rule against granting security for judgment.

From canvassing the case law, I find that an order preserving the assets of one party is available: 1. where there are no assets in the jurisdiction against which to enforce a judgment and the appeal has little merit (Vaccaro at para 11

Richland Construction Inc v Manningwa Developments Inc., 1996 CarswellBC 1767 (WL Can) at paras 12-13 (CA)); 2. to preserve assets that would otherwise be destroyed, disposed of, or dissipated prior to the resolution of the dispute (Hamza at paras 26–30; 1400467 Alberta Ltd v Adderley, 2014 ABQB 439 at para 52, 591 AR 40
Aetna Financial at 12); and 3. to encourage respect for the judicial process and avoid abuse of process (Hamza at para 23, citing Mooney v Orr
(2d) 335 at 348 (BCSC) [Mooney cited in this judgment to 1994 CarswellBC 26 (WL Can)]; Vaccaro at paras 12–14; Aetna Financial at 12).

25 The exception that I am most concerned with in this application is encouraging respect for the judicial process and avoiding abuse of process and, to a lesser extent, avoiding the disposition of assets prior to ultimate resolution.

As Huddart J. stated in Mooney at paragraphs 66–69: • A litigant cannot be permitted to use the court to his advantage while effectively disavowing in advance any judgment against him … (the ordering of the security is) not to enhance the claimant's rights, but to ensure that those reasonable people who pay for the administration of justice in this province are not affronted by the impotence of the court in the face of those who choose to order their affairs so as to keep all their options for themselves.
Rule is Constitutional In Trisura Guarantee Insurance v.
Duchnij, et al., 2021 ABCA 78, 2021 CarswellAlta 461, 26 Alta.
(6th) 6, Justice Wakeling said, at paragraph 10: [10] Rule 14.67 of the Alberta Rules of Court is not inconsistent with the Constitution Act, 1867. …

Filing Appeal Does Not Act as Stay … an appeal does not operate as a stay of execution unless a court so directs, so that simply filing a notice of appeal has no effect on the previous order. Dominion Construction Ltd. v. C.F.L. Forming Ltd. (1982), 23 Alta. L.R. (2d) 239 (Q.B.), at 242, per Cawsey J. Veit J. said: The general Alberta rule is that a mere appeal does not operate as a stay. MacDonald v. P.P.F., Local 488 (1990), 77 Alta. L.R. (2d) 56 at 58 (Q.B.). The Court of Appeal has stated: I would just point out that according to r. 508 an appeal does not of itself operate as any kind of stay of anything. Canada (Attorney General) v. Doz (Samuel) Professional Corp. (1992), 125 A.R. 236 at 237 (C.A.). And: … the Courts are usually reluctant to give a stay of a money judgment; that is why the Alberta Rules do not call for an automatic stay pending appeal. It seems to me that the fact that the defendant lacks assets is not a reason to stay execution. If execution will be futile, then it can do the defendant no harm and it will test his assertion than he has little in the way of assets. The exemptions laws in Alberta give additional protection to a debtor. Acheson v. Dory (1993), 15 Alta. L.R. (3d) 43 (C.A.), at 44, per Côté J.A. In Strathcona (County) v. Half Moon Lake Resort Ltd. (2000), 275 A.R. 185 (Q.B.), Ritter J. set out the general rule, and then outlined an exception. Dory (1993), 149 A.R. 71, 63 W.A.C. 71 (C.A.)). This is, however, only the “normal rule” and there are exceptions to it. I am satisfied that one of those exceptions may be based on practicality. Rana, 2022 ABCA 378, 2022 CarswellAlta 3321, leave to appeal refused 2023 CarswellAlta 810 (S.C.C.), the Court said: [5] Rule 14.74(b) of the Rules of Court permits a panel of the Court of Appeal to dismiss all or part of an appeal if the appeal is moot. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.75:1 Rule 14.75 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.75. 1. Test for New Evidence The test that should be applied to persuade an appeal court to allow new evidence has been well established by the cases. The tests are set out very well in Schiff in Evidence in the Litigation Process (2nd Ed.), and I quote as follows: Accordingly to the standard approved by the Supreme Court of Canada for civil cases, absent very unusual circumstances, Canadian appellate courts will grant the applicant's request to present new evidence only if two conditions are satisfied: first, the applicant could not have obtained the evidence by reasonable diligence before the trial and, second, the evidence is of such nature that, if introduced before the appellate court and at a new trial, it would be practically conclusive to cause reversal of the original result. Gorrie v. Nielson (1988), 92 A.R. 164 at 165 (C.A.). The Court of Appeal restated the test in Reform Party of Canada v. Canada (Attorney General) (1995), 27 Alta. L.R. (3d) 153, at pp. 185–86: In Palmer v. R., [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759, the Supreme Court of Canada set out the following criteria for the admission of fresh evidence (at p. 775): (1) The evidence should generally not be admitted if, by due diligence, it could have been adduced at trial provided that this general principle will not be applied as strictly in a criminal case as in civil cases … (2) The evidence must be relevant in the sense that it bears upon a decisive or potentially decisive issue in the trial. (3) The evidence must be credible in the sense that it is reasonably capable of belief, and (4) It must be such that if believed it could reasonably, when taken with the other evidence adduced at trial, be expected to have affected the result. The Court of Appeal set forth the same test in R. v. Blair (1995), 174 A.R. 307 at 309 (C.A.). The obligation to exercise reasonable diligence in putting the evidence before the court extends up to the time judgment is actually rendered (and most likely up to the time of entry). On applications to admit fresh evidence on appeal, this Court will look at whether or not the evidence could have been obtained and might have been introduced by reasonable diligence at any time prior to the final judgment. Public School Boards' Assn. (Alberta) v. Alberta (Attorney-General) (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 62 (C.A.), at 78, per Russell J.A. [additional reasons at (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 390 (C.A.)]. Further, the rule for new evidence is a general rule. However, the two part test is nothing more than a general rule. On occasion, this Court has seen fit to adopt a more flexible approach to the admission of fresh evidence, even if that evidence is not practically conclusive. Public School Boards' Assn. (Alberta) v. Alberta (Attorney-General) (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 62 (C.A.), at 78, per Russell J.A. [additional reasons at (1998), 64 Alta. L.R. (3d) 390 (C.A.); leave to appeal allowed (1998), 232 A.R. 200 (note) S.C.C.; leave to appeal refused (1999), 237 A.R. 200 (note) (S.C.C.); affirmed (2000), 85 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1 (S.C.C.)]. In Fougere v. The King’s University, 2024 ABCA 183, Justice Feehan discussed applications for leave to introduce new evidence in an appeal: [9] As set out in P & C Lawfirm Management Inc v Sabourin, 2020 ABCA 285, para 11, former rule 516.2 expressly required a party to obtain leave to apply to introduce new evidence if the application had not been made before the party’s factum was due. The current rule does not include an express provision to the same effect, but this Court requires applications for permission to file late new evidence under the rule. Relevant considerations include the reason for the late filing, the effect of the late filing on the appeal proper, and whether the application for new evidence has a reasonable prospect of success or is prima facie meritorious: P & C Lawfirm, para 12; R v Gendreau, 2011 ABCA 256, para 32. [10] Leave has been denied where the application for new evidence had no reasonable prospect of success: Gendreau, para 33 (the fresh evidence was only marginally relevant or material); Belland v Belland, 2008 ABCA 226, para 6 (the fresh evidence was irrelevant); Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 28, para 13, 380 AR 340 (the fresh evidence was not arguably probative). The threshold for granting a leave application is necessarily low, although irrelevant evidence cannot meet any threshold: Belland, para 6. 2. Raising a New Issue on Appeal In Haloute v. Montpetit (2004), 35 Alta. L.R. (4th) 1 (C.A.), Ritter J.A. said, at p. 3: This Court recently affirmed in Alberta (Minister of Public Works, Supply & Services) v. Nilsson (2002), 8 Alta. L.R. (4th) 83 (Alta C.A.) at paras. 169–175, that an appellant is entitled to raise a new issue on appeal only when all material evidence is before the court and the respondent has not been prejudiced by the course taken by the appellant. The burden on the party seeking to raise the new issue is substantial. The party must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that (1) all the facts relevant to the new argument are before the appellate court …; and (2) the opposing party could not have led additional evidence relevant to the new argument had it been raised at trial. … In Wasylynuk v. Bouma, 2019 ABCA 234, 2019 CarswellAlta 1109, 89 Alta. L.R. (6th) 88, the Court said: [11] The general rule is that where an issue was not raised in the pleadings or argued before the trial judge, it cannot be a ground of appeal: 681210 Alberta Ltd v Hunter, 2012 ABCA 83 (CanLII) at para 25, 522 AR 109. An appellate court should not entertain an issue raised for the first time on appeal unless it is apparent that no further light could have been shed upon the question had it been raised at the proper time: Quan v Cusson, 2009 SCC 62 (CanLII) at para 36, [2009] 3 SCR 712; Haloute v Montpetit, 2004 ABCA 263 (CanLII) at para 6, 354 AR 397. 3. Findings of Fact The Court of Appeal may not interfere with findings of fact absent palpable and overriding error. The appellant contends that neither the Court of Appeal nor this court should interfere with the findings of fact made by the Board of Inquiry or the Court of Queen's Bench. In support of this view, reliance is placed on the common law principle of curial deference to findings of fact made by a court of first instance. In Stein v. “Kathy K” (The) (“Storm Point” (The)), [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802 … Ritchie J. wrote at p. 808 [S.C.R.]: These authorities are not to be taken as meaning that the findings of fact made at trial are immutable, but rather that they are not to be reversed unless it can be established that the learned trial judge made some palpable and overriding error which affected his assessment of the facts. … The common law position set out above is echoed in R. 518 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 390/68, which restricts the Court of Appeal's jurisdiction to review trial courts on questions of law or inferences drawn from the facts. Following this rule, the appellate court may not interfere with findings of fact except in cases in which the trier of fact has made a palpable and overriding error. University of Alberta v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission) ((1992),), 4 Alta. L.R. (3d) 193 at 207-208 (S.C.C.). The Supreme Court of Canada restated its position in Toneguzzo-Norvell (Guardian ad litem of) v. Burnaby Hospital, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 114. At pp. 121–22, Madam Justice McLachlin, speaking for the court, said: It is by now well-established that a Court of Appeal must not interfere with a trial judge's conclusions on matters of fact unless there is palpable or overriding error. In principle, a Court of Appeal will only interfere if the judge has made a manifest error, has ignored conclusive or relevant evidence, has misunderstood the evidence, or has drawn erroneous conclusions from it … A Court of Appeal is clearly not entitled to interfere merely because it takes a different view of the evidence. The finding of facts and the drawing of evidentiary conclusions from facts is the province of the trial judge, not the Court of Appeal … I agree that the principle of non-intervention of a Court of Appeal in a trial judge's findings of facts does not apply with the same force to inferences drawn from conflicting testimony of expert witnesses where the credibility of these witnesses is not in issue. Costs Judgment Rule 520 says that interest runs from the date of trial judgment on a new or amended appellate judgment for a sum of money. If that does not apply directly to a costs judgment, then it would have to apply by close analogy under R. 4. The general principle of appeals is that the appeal court gives the judgment which the trial judge should have given. Indeed, it is certified to the Clerk and enforced as a Queen's Bench judgment: R. 528(2). Anything else would be unfair. We repeat that the interest in question is on Queen's Bench costs. And of course the plaintiff who is to pay the costs has had the use of the money in the interval. And post-judgment interest rates are vey low now anyway; they are far lower than a business could earn on its capital. So post-judgment interest on the Queen's Bench costs should run from the date of pronouncement of the Queen's Bench judgment…Ed Miller Sales & Rentals Ltd. v. Caterpillar Tractor Co. (1998), 61 Alta. L.R. (3d) 256 (C.A.), at 260, per curiam[additional reasons to (1996), 41 Alta. L.R. (3d) 217 C.A.; leave to appeal refused (1997), 209 A.R. 400n (S.C.C.)]. 2. Interest on Reversal The jurisprudence holds that an Appellant who has satisfied a judgment for the payment of money is entitled, on the reversal of the judgment, to repayment together with interest … These cases also sugges that the repayment ordered included repayment of pre-judgment interest. Colborne Capital Corp. v. 542775 Alberta Ltd. (1999), 74 Alta. L.R. (3d) 263 (C.A.), at 267, per curiam. Interest also accrues on costs which are to repaid because of a reversal at appeal. In Hanke v. Resurfice Corp. (2006), 58 Alta. L.R. (4th) 14 (C.A.); reversed 2007 SCC 7, 2007 CarswellAlta 130, [2007] 1 S.C.R. 333, 404 A.R. 333, the Court said, at pp. 17–18: Costs were the subject of the trial judgment in this case. In our view, that judgment is a “judgment debt” pursuant to s. 6 of the Judgment Interest Act. … This Court has also held that “when an appeal court upsets a judgment already paid, the repayment carries interest”: Severin v. Veale (2000), 261 A.R. 369, ¶ 10 (Alta. C.A.). See also Colborne Capital Corp. v. 542775 Alberta Ltd. (1999), 250 A.R. 79 (Alta. C.A.). … there is “no valid reason” why costs should not also carry interest. We conclude, accordingly, that there is no reason in principle to fail to award interest on a refund of costs in the case at bar. On appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada ([2007] S.C.J. No. 7), the Court allowed the appeal and restored the trial judgment which had found no liability on the part of the defendant. Accordingly, the Supreme Court of Canada did not comment on the above quotation. It should still be considered the view of the Court of Appeal on the topic.

Extensions in Cases of Short Delays It is not necessary to show absence of prejudice in a case where the delay is only a day or so: we draw an inference from such a short delay that there is no prejudice. Similarly, we do not require in cases of such short delay that an arguable case be established. Cascade Development Corp. v. Red Deer College (1991), 115 A.R. 325 (C.A.), at 326, per Kerans J.A. Respondent aware of, but not served with, notice of appeal In R. v. Sharifi-Jamali, 2022 ABCA 114, 2022 CarswellAlta 801, the Crown wanted to appeal a sentence imposed on December 16, 2021, on Mr. Sharifi-Jamali. The deadline for service of the notice of appeal was January 17, 2022. Delays over the Christmas break meant that formal approval within the Crown's office to file the appeal was not obtained until January 10, 2022. Difficulties with the Court of Appeal's electronic filing system (CAMS) delayed the filing of the notice of appeal until January 13, 2022. Though not authorized by a court order, service of the notice of appeal was made on the respondent's fiancée on January 17, 2022, and on the same day a text was sent to the respondent's telephone notifying him of notice of appeal and asking if the document could be sent to him by email. The respondent suggested receiving the documents on January 21 when he would be back in Calgary (he was working out of Calgary). A further offer to email the documents did not receive a response from the respondent. The Court of Appeal granted the Crown's application for an order “confirming that service in this case is good and sufficient.” The Court said: [8] Service of the respondent is a fundamental step in the appeal process, but service is essentially a question of fact. The key is that the existence of the legal proceedings must be brought to the attention of the respondent or defendant, in circumstances in which it is clear that legal rights are to be engaged: Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corp, 2012 ABCA 266 at paras. 17–19, 542 AR 12. On this record it is clear that the respondent knew, within the deadline of January 17, that an appeal had been launched, and that his legal rights were engaged. It is true that he had not received an actual copy of the notice of appeal, but one was offered to him, and it is not evident that he would have done anything differently if he had received an actual copy. He has suffered no prejudice as a result of the irregularities in the service. [9] The respondent correctly points out that the procedure used by the Public Prosecution Service of Canada to approve an appeal is complex, and will inherently use up some of the time in which an appeal must be served. Lack of diligence is one factor to be weighed, but it is difficult to criticize the appellant for being careful: R. v Chan, 2012 ABCA 250 at paras. 33-36, 536 AR 159. Being careful is not the same thing as an absence of diligence. In this case, some delay was occasioned by the Christmas break, and the problems with the CAMS system. It is not unreasonable for members of the Bar to be away from their offices over the Christmas holiday. [10] Since the appeal came to the attention of the respondent within the appeal period, it is not strictly necessary to apply the test for extending the time in R. v Roberge, 2005 SCC 48 at para. 6, [2005] 2 SCR 469. [11] The respondent also notes that substitutional service was attempted on him, but without a prior order approving that. Where there is ample time, obtaining an order for substitutional service is usually the preferable procedure. However, when time begins to run out, it is often a more practical approach to attempt substitutional service, in the hope and expectation that it will successfully bring the appeal to the attention of the respondent. Contrary to the suggestion in R. v Nguyen, 2016 ABCA 410 at para. 39, 47 Alta LR (6th) 108, the absence of a prior substitutional service order does not render the process less effective or less fair when the notice of appeal actually comes to the attention of the respondent. Further, the Court of Appeal does not have an easily accessible procedure for obtaining substitutional service orders on very short notice. [12] In this case the appellant could have acted more expeditiously, but the respondent had notice of the appeal within the appeal period. He has suffered no prejudice, and the Public Prosecution Service of Canada is entitled to an order confirming that service in this case is good and sufficient.

39, 47 Alta LR (6th) 108, the absence of a prior substitutional service order does not render the process less effective or less fair when the notice of appeal actually comes to the attention of the respondent.
Further, the Court of Appeal does not have an easily accessible procedure for obtaining substitutional service orders on very short notice.
[12] In this case the appellant could have acted more expeditiously, but the respondent had notice of the appeal within the appeal period.
He has suffered no prejudice, and the Public Prosecution Service of Canada is entitled to an order confirming that service in this case is good and sufficient.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.88:1 Rule 14.88 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.88. In Vallieres v. Vozniak, 2014 ABCA 384, 2014 CarswellAlta 2096, 6 Alta. L.R. (6th) 35, 47 R.P.R. (5th) 209, the Court commented on costs awards on appeals (at paragraphs 4, 7, and 8): [4] Costs of appeals are dealt with based on certain well-established principles: (a) Unless another order is made, the successful party on the appeal is entitled to costs: R. 14.88(1). (b) The Court frequently will not make any specific direction as to costs, relying on the presumption that the successful party on the appeal is entitled to costs: Information Note following R. 14.88. (c) Unless another order is made, the costs on appeal are assessed on the same scale as those directed at trial: R. 14.88(3). Departures from these presumptions are sometimes required, for example where the trial judgment is reversed, where formal offers of settlement have been made, or where other circumstances dictate a different costs order. Preliminary directions as to costs, such as those found in the reasons resolving this appeal, can be varied if further information (e.g., the existence of formal offers) is brought forward. Costs can be spoken to at any time: R. 10.30(1). … [7] The appellants argue that they are entitled to solicitor and client costs based on a covenant in the real estate contract: 9. If the Seller or the Buyer fails or refuses to complete this contract according to its terms, then the other party may pursue all available remedies. The Seller's remedies include keeping the Deposit and claiming additional damages. Both the Seller and the Buyer can claim reasonable costs including legal fees and disbursements on a solicitor/client full indemnity basis. Costs are presumptively assessed on Schedule C, but a contract providing for a different scale of costs is a recognized exception to that general rule: Trinier v Shurnaik, 2011 ABCA 314 (CanLII) at paras. 39–42, 68 Alta LR (5th) 400; 515 AR 148; Collins v Collin, 2005 ABCA 98 (CanLII) at para. 15, 363 AR 229. [8] The respondent argues that solicitor and client costs are not available on this appeal because the trial judge only ordered costs on Column 3. He argues, in effect, that the presumption in R. 14.88(3) that appeal costs are on the same scale as trial costs prevails over the rule that solicitor and client costs will generally be awarded when provided for in a contract. Rule 14.88(3), however, only creates a presumption, and it can be displaced when the context requires. In particular, when the trial judgment is set aside, any ruling on costs is generally also subject to adjustment. Here the trial judgment was reversed, justifying a reversal of the resulting costs award. In Walton v. Alberta (Securities Commission), 2014 ABCA 446, 2014 CarswellAlta 2381, the Court said, at paragraphs 3–4: [3] Two of the successful appellants seek costs of the appeal. Rule 14.88 provides that the successful party is presumptively entitled to costs. It also provides that the scale of costs is presumed to be the one that “applies to the order or judgment appealed from”. It is not always clear how the latter presumption applies to appeals from administrative tribunals. [4] Because of the presumptions found in R. 14.88, the Information Note after that rule observes that the Court will generally not find it necessary to give any specific direction on costs. Rule 10.30 confirms, however, that costs can be spoken to at any time, and the Information Note allows an application for a ruling on costs if made within two months of the pronouncement of the decision. Rule 14.25(1)(f) requires that the request for any special direction with respect to costs be included in the factums, but the failure to do so can be excused if there is no prejudice: R. 1.5(4). In Enmax Energy Corp. v. TransAlta Generation Partnership, 2016 ABCA 263, 2016 CarswellAlta 1701, the Court stated again that the default rule (costs of the appeal follow the result) will apply unless counsel seek a different direction, and that any such request must be made within two months of the pronouncement of the decision. The Court said: 4 The successful appellant also seeks costs of the appeal. Reasons for judgment issued by the Court generally do not deal with costs. The Court relies on the default rule that costs of the appeal follow the result, at the same scale as that awarded in the trial court: R. 14.88. The Information Note after R. 14.88 summarizes: Information Note: Reasons for judgment of the Court of Appeal will not make any specific direction about costs unless an exception is to be made to the presumption in rule 14.88(1) that the successful party is entitled to costs of the appeal. Any request for a specific direction as to costs must be made within two months of the pronouncement of the decision. The Reasons for Judgment in this appeal were filed on December 9, 2015, and the request for a ruling on costs was received eight months later on August 12, 2016. 5 While the two month limit in the Information Note can be relaxed under R. 13.5(2), no sufficient reason has been advanced why that should be done in this case. The appellant submits that the delay resulted from an unsuccessful application by the respondent for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, but such an application is no reason to delay finalizing proceedings in the Court of Appeal. Whether or not leave is granted, the Alberta Court of Appeal proceedings must be finalized, the formal judgment must be entered, and costs must be dealt with. 6 It is now too late for the parties to seek specific directions on costs: Trosin v Sikora, 2006 ABCA 399. The parties have, by reason of delay, disentitled themselves to any element of costs that requires a specific direction of the Court. Accordingly, the costs of the appeal must be assessed based on the presumptions in the Rules. The successful appellant is entitled to assessed costs, and since no scale of costs was specified by the chambers judge, Column 1 of Schedule C applies. Also see: Y. (T.L.) v. Y. (M.L.), 2016 ABCA 264, 2016 CarswellAlta 1698 in which the two month limit in the Information Note was invoked by the Court. In Turner v. Bell Mobility Inc., 2016 ABCA 188, 2016 CarswellAlta 1123, the Court discussed costs, and in particular, R. 14.88: 5 This rule [Rule 14.88] also conveys a general policy that the unsuccessful party should expect to pay costs. In MacCabe v Westlock Roman Catholic Separate School District No 110, 2002 ABCA 307, at para 3, 320 AR 194 it was held that this Court had jurisdiction to vary trial costs: “This Court has jurisdiction to determine the costs at trial as a result of an appeal: Caterpillar Tractor Co. v. Ed Miller Sales and Rentals Ltd., [1998] 10 W.W.R. 736.”. 6 In MacCabe, the first instance decision was altered by this Court as to the quantum of damages to be received by the plaintiff after a discount for contributory negligence, but this Court also noted that the trial occupied 27 days and was “neither simple nor short” and a large number of issues involving liability as well as damages were determined by reference to numerous witnesses and experts. In the end, this Court determined the appeal costs to reflect the outcome here, but held that it would not be “fair or just to vary the trial costs” based on a number of considerations. In other words, MacCabe demonstrates that the exercise of the jurisdiction of this Court as to costs at trial may involve a constellation of considerations including at para 13 “the difficulty of the case, the length of time involved, behaviour of the parties, importance of the issues and other factors”. 7 Another factor is whether the success was on procedural or substantive issues: Jackson v. Trimac Ltd. (1994) 155 AR 42 at para 29. Another factor arises from offers of compromise: Eagle Resources Ltd v MacDonald, 2006 ABCA 49, 380 AR 333. If an appellant does not ask for costs in their pleadings on appeal, the Court has discretion to refuse to give them: West Edmonton Mall v McDonald's Restaurants of Canada Ltd, (1993) 145 AR 76 at para 2. That discretion might well be activated wholly or partly if the post-appeal request for reversed costs below has a serious unfairness element, but it should be recalled that the presumption under both the Court of Queen's Bench and Court of Appeal Rules, as noted above, is that the unsuccessful party should pay. So there cannot be any surprise emanating from the Court Rules on this subject. 8 The fact of no surprise remains even if the costs of trial do not automatically flow and must be awarded, if appropriate, to a successful appellant: see MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 354 at para 6, 401 AR 10. A key decision interpreting Rule 14.88, which suggests that the principle of costs following the event remains, is Vallieres v Vozniak, 2014 ABCA 384 at paras 5 and 6, 588 AR 17 which summarizes as follows: 5 The appellants argue that they, as the successful litigants, are entitled to assessed costs of both the trial and the appeal, and, as a result of a covenant in the agreement, all on a solicitor and client basis. Alternatively, they seek a doubling of costs after certain formal offers were made. The respondent concedes that the appellants are entitled to costs, but argues that they are limited to Column 3 of Schedule C, being the scale of costs awarded by the trial judge. The respondent also concedes that certain offers would have the effect of doubling some of the costs. 6 The appellants were successful on the appeal, and there is no basis on which to deny them their assessed costs. Further, since the trial decision was reversed, the appellants are also entitled to costs of the trial: R. 10.29. 1. Costs: What Constitutes Being the “Successful” Party? In Mahe v. Boulianne, 2010 ABCA 74, 2010 CarswellAlta 396, 21 Alta. L.R. (5th) 277, the Court said, at paragraph 6: 6 The general rule is that the successful party on appeal is entitled to costs of the appeal. It is rare for any successful party on appeal to be successful on each and every argument that is made. Where several forms of relief are requested on appeal, it is also relatively rare for the successful party to succeed on each item of relief. Further, the parties often make arguments on points that the court does not have to deal with, because of the way the decision unfolds. The general rule contemplates that the party who achieves substantial success on the appeal will receive costs, even if that party is not totally successful, nor successful on every issue or argument. Generally the costs follow the ultimate result, and costs are not usually apportioned on an issue-by-issue basis, a claim-by-claim basis or on a head-of-damages basis, although there is a discretion to do that in proper cases: Wilde v. Archean Energy Ltd., 2008 ABCA 132, 88 Alta. L.R. (4th) 54, 429 A.R. 41 at para. 9; Sutherland v. Canada (Attorney General), 2008 BCCA 27 at para. 7; British Columbia v. Worthington (Canada) Inc., [1989] 1 W.W.R. 1, 29 B.C.L.R. (2d) 145, 32 C.P.C. (2d) 166 (B.C.C.A.); Portugal Cove-St. Phillips (Town) v. Willcott (1997), 150 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 183, 20 C.P.C. (4th) 237 (Nfld. C.A.) at paras. 13–19. In this case the appellant was substantially successful by reducing the amount of the damage award by a significant amount, and he is entitled to costs of the appeal: Alberta Wheat Pool v. Northwest Pile Driving Ltd., 2000 BCCA 641, 146 B.C.A.C. 119, 2 C.P.C. (5th) 12 at paras. 18-9. 864 In Hogarth v. Rocky Mountain Slate Inc., 2013 ABCA 116, 2013 CarswellAlta 835, 87 Alta. L.R. (5th) 108, the Court said, at paragraph 12: 12 On appeal, the appellant Simonson was successful in having the entire judgment against him set aside. As such, he is entitled to assessed costs of the appeal. The respondents argue that Simonson should not receive full, or any costs, because he was not successful on all of the arguments that he raised. Costs, however, are not usually allocated on an issue by issue basis: Mahe v. Boulianne, 2010 ABCA 74 at para. 6, 21 Alta LR (5th) 277. It is rare for a litigant to be successful on each and every issue, but that does not mean that litigants should not argue every issue reasonably raised on the record, nor does that disentitle them to costs. At the end of the day Simonson was successful on appeal in having the entire judgment set aside, and he is entitled to costs. See also: Johannson v. Haaranen, 2019 ABCA 197, 2019 CarswellAlta 956 at paragraph 4. 2. Costs on an Application to Seek Permission to Appeal In Liquor Store Limited Partnership v. Edmonton (City), 2018 ABCA 34, 2018 CarswellAlta 135, Liquor Store Limited Partnership successfully sought permission to appeal a decision of the Edmonton Subdivision and Development Appeal Board, but ultimately was unsuccessful in the appeal. The successful respondent on the actual appeal (Mr. Aggarwal) sought costs of the appeal and costs of the leave to appeal application (which he had unsuccessfully opposed). The Court granted the respondent costs of both the appeal and the leave to appeal application. The Court said: 5 Mr. Noce, Q.C., counsel for Liquor Stores, argues that his client is entitled to its costs on the permission-to-appeal application, as it was the successful party, and to set off these costs against those to which Mr. Aggarwal is entitled, on account of his success on the appeal. He maintains that the disjunctive “or” in r. 14.88(1) supports his position.5 6 We agree with Mr. Murphy that his client is entitled to its costs. It is the successful party on the appeal. Because the permission-to-appeal application is an integral part of the appeal process, Mr. Aggarwal is entitled to his costs for opposing the permission-to-appeal application.6 7 An unsuccessful applicant for permission to appeal must pay the respondent's costs. This is because the unsuccessful application brings the appeal process to an end and the respondent is undoubtedly the successful party. 8 For the same reason, an appellant who secures permission to appeal but loses the appeal must pay the respondent's costs.7 The disposition of the appeal ends the appeal process and the respondent is the successful party.8 Costs of a successful permission-to-appeal application are, in effect, in the cause. 3. Time period within which to apply for costs in an amount other than default costs In Oslanski v. Oslanski, 2021 ABCA 68, 2021 CarswellAlta 366, Justice Wakeling considered the time period within one must apply for a costs order in an amount different from that set by the default rule. His Lordship said: [52] Rule 14.88 does not expressly stipulate the period within which a party to an appeal may seek a costs ruling different than the default rule set out in rule 14.88(1)—the successful party is entitled to a costs award from the unsuccessful party on the same scale that applies to the order appealed from. … [63]… A party must apply for a direction under rule 14.88 within two months of the pronouncement of the decision unless the party adverse in interest to the applicant agrees to a reasonable extension of time or the applicant has a compelling reason for missing the deadline if there is no agreement. 4. Costs on Unsuccessful Applications to Reopen Appeals In Piikani Nation v. Kostic, 2018 ABCA 320, 2018 CarswellAlta 2125, 75 Alta. L.R. (6th) 30, [2018] 11 W.W.R. 38, the Court said: [6] As a deterrent to applications to reopen appeals, generous costs awards are made when such applications are unsuccessful: Eagle Resources Ltd. v MacDonald, 2002 ABCA 12 (CanLII) at para. 10, 96 Alta LR (3d) 12, 299 AR 395. 5. Inadequate trial costs are not an argument for increased appeal costs In Geophysical Service Incorporated v. Falkland Oil and Gas Limited, 2020 ABCA 106, 2020 CarswellAlta 751, Geophysical sued Falkland and sought $17.6M in damages. That action was summarily dismissed, and costs were awarded to Falkland (the successful defendant). Geophysical's appeal was dismissed, and Falkland sought appeal costs at a higher rate than that awarded at the trial level. One of the submissions in support of higher costs was that “the trial costs award was inadequate.” On the basis of other factors, the Court of Appeal ultimately awarded appeal costs at a slightly higher rate than those awarded in the trial court (double Column 5 increased by 45.6% for inflation, as opposed to 1.5 times Column 5 increased by 45.6%). However, the Court of Appeal specifically stated: [5] The respondent argues in part that it should receive enhanced costs of the appeal, because the trial costs award was inadequate. Any shortcomings in the trial costs award should have been dealt with by a direct appeal. 6. Revisiting trial costs after successful appeal In Dunn v. Condominium Corporation No. 042 0105, 2024 ABCA 103, after the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal from a trial judge’s decision, the successful Appellant asked the Court of Appeal to revisit the trial costs decision. The Court of Appeal decided that each party should bear its own costs at the trial level. The Court gave this summary of the law: [5] When the result at trial is reversed on appeal, the basis for the costs award at trial disappears and this Court can revisit the matter of trial costs, even if there was no error as to trial costs: MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 354 at para 8 citing FFM Holdings Ltd v Lilydale Co-operative Limited, 2002 ABCA 113. The presumption in r 10.29 that the party who enjoys substantial success at trial will be entitled to costs against the unsuccessful party continues to apply and successful appellants usually are also entitled to trial costs: Vallieres v Vozniak, 2014 ABCA 384 at para 6, cited in Turner v Bell Mobility, 2016 ABCA 188 at para 8. [6] In rare circumstances, trial courts will exercise their discretion to award costs against a successful party, for example where there has been misconduct, or in significant public interest cases: Mark Orkin, The Law of Costs, 2nd Ed (Aurora: Canada Law Book, 2007 – Proview) at § 2:39 and cases cited therein, Stubicar v Calgary (City) Subdivision and Development Appeal Board, 2023 ABCA 98 at paras 50-51 (single judge). This Court may choose not to disturb an award of costs at trial in favour of a losing party in a case involving special and peculiar problems: 321665 Alberta Ltd v Husky Oil Operations Ltd, 2013 ABCA 326 at para 5, citing Alberta Public Schools Association v Alberta (Attorney General), 1998 ABCA 238, 216 AR 249 at paras 17 and 20. [7] This Court’s discretion to award costs must be exercised judicially. …

6 It is now too late for the parties to seek specific directions on costs: Trosin v Sikora, 2006 ABCA 399.
The parties have, by reason of delay, disentitled themselves to any element of costs that requires a specific direction of the Court.
Accordingly, the costs of the appeal must be assessed based on the presumptions in the Rules.
The successful appellant is entitled to assessed costs, and since no scale of costs was specified by the chambers judge, Column 1 of Schedule C applies.

Bell Mobility Inc., 2016 ABCA 188, 2016 CarswellAlta 1123, the Court discussed costs, and in particular, R.
14.88: 5 This rule [Rule 14.88] also conveys a general policy that the unsuccessful party should expect to pay costs.

In MacCabe v Westlock Roman Catholic Separate School District No 110, 2002 ABCA 307, at para 3, 320 AR 194 it was held that this Court had jurisdiction to vary trial costs: “This Court has jurisdiction to determine the costs at trial as a result of an appeal: Caterpillar Tractor Co. v.
Ed Miller Sales and Rentals Ltd., [1998] 10 W.W.R.

6 In MacCabe, the first instance decision was altered by this Court as to the quantum of damages to be received by the plaintiff after a discount for contributory negligence, but this Court also noted that the trial occupied 27 days and was “neither simple nor short” and a large number of issues involving liability as well as damages were determined by reference to numerous witnesses and experts.
In the end, this Court determined the appeal costs to reflect the outcome here, but held that it would not be “fair or just to vary the trial costs” based on a number of considerations.

In other words, MacCabe demonstrates that the exercise of the jurisdiction of this Court as to costs at trial may involve a constellation of considerations including at para 13 “the difficulty of the case, the length of time involved, behaviour of the parties, importance of the issues and other factors”.
7 Another factor is whether the success was on procedural or substantive issues: Jackson v.
Another factor arises from offers of compromise: Eagle Resources Ltd v MacDonald, 2006 ABCA 49, 380 AR 333.

If an appellant does not ask for costs in their pleadings on appeal, the Court has discretion to refuse to give them: West Edmonton Mall v McDonald's Restaurants of Canada Ltd, (1993) 145 AR 76 at para 2.

That discretion might well be activated wholly or partly if the post-appeal request for reversed costs below has a serious unfairness element, but it should be recalled that the presumption under both the Court of Queen's Bench and Court of Appeal Rules, as noted above, is that the unsuccessful party should pay.
So there cannot be any surprise emanating from the Court Rules on this subject.

8 The fact of no surprise remains even if the costs of trial do not automatically flow and must be awarded, if appropriate, to a successful appellant: see MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 354 at para 6, 401 AR 10.

A key decision interpreting Rule 14.88, which suggests that the principle of costs following the event remains, is Vallieres v Vozniak, 2014 ABCA 384 at paras 5 and 6, 588 AR 17 which summarizes as follows: 5 The appellants argue that they, as the successful litigants, are entitled to assessed costs of both the trial and the appeal, and, as a result of a covenant in the agreement, all on a solicitor and client basis.
Alternatively, they seek a doubling of costs after certain formal offers were made.
The respondent concedes that the appellants are entitled to costs, but argues that they are limited to Column 3 of Schedule C, being the scale of costs awarded by the trial judge.
The respondent also concedes that certain offers would have the effect of doubling some of the costs.
6 The appellants were successful on the appeal, and there is no basis on which to deny them their assessed costs.
Further, since the trial decision was reversed, the appellants are also entitled to costs of the trial: R.
Costs: What Constitutes Being the “Successful” Party?
(5th) 277, the Court said, at paragraph 6: 6 The general rule is that the successful party on appeal is entitled to costs of the appeal.
It is rare for any successful party on appeal to be successful on each and every argument that is made.
Where several forms of relief are requested on appeal, it is also relatively rare for the successful party to succeed on each item of relief.
Further, the parties often make arguments on points that the court does not have to deal with, because of the way the decision unfolds.

The general rule contemplates that the party who achieves substantial success on the appeal will receive costs, even if that party is not totally successful, nor successful on every issue or argument.

Generally the costs follow the ultimate result, and costs are not usually apportioned on an issue-by-issue basis, a claim-by-claim basis or on a head-of-damages basis, although there is a discretion to do that in proper cases: Wilde v.
In this case the appellant was substantially successful by reducing the amount of the damage award by a significant amount, and he is entitled to costs of the appeal: Alberta Wheat Pool v.
Northwest Pile Driving Ltd., 2000 BCCA 641, 146 B.C.A.C.
Rocky Mountain Slate Inc., 2013 ABCA 116, 2013 CarswellAlta 835, 87 Alta.
(5th) 108, the Court said, at paragraph 12: 12 On appeal, the appellant Simonson was successful in having the entire judgment against him set aside.
As such, he is entitled to assessed costs of the appeal.
The respondents argue that Simonson should not receive full, or any costs, because he was not successful on all of the arguments that he raised.
Costs, however, are not usually allocated on an issue by issue basis: Mahe v.

It is rare for a litigant to be successful on each and every issue, but that does not mean that litigants should not argue every issue reasonably raised on the record, nor does that disentitle them to costs.
At the end of the day Simonson was successful on appeal in having the entire judgment set aside, and he is entitled to costs.
Costs on an Application to Seek Permission to Appeal In Liquor Store Limited Partnership v.

Edmonton (City), 2018 ABCA 34, 2018 CarswellAlta 135, Liquor Store Limited Partnership successfully sought permission to appeal a decision of the Edmonton Subdivision and Development Appeal Board, but ultimately was unsuccessful in the appeal.
The successful respondent on the actual appeal (Mr.
Aggarwal) sought costs of the appeal and costs of the leave to appeal application (which he had unsuccessfully opposed).
The Court granted the respondent costs of both the appeal and the leave to appeal application.

Noce, Q.C., counsel for Liquor Stores, argues that his client is entitled to its costs on the permission-to-appeal application, as it was the successful party, and to set off these costs against those to which Mr.
Aggarwal is entitled, on account of his success on the appeal.
He maintains that the disjunctive “or” in r.
14.88(1) supports his position.5 6 We agree with Mr.
Murphy that his client is entitled to its costs.
It is the successful party on the appeal.
Because the permission-to-appeal application is an integral part of the appeal process, Mr.
Aggarwal is entitled to his costs for opposing the permission-to-appeal application.6 7 An unsuccessful applicant for permission to appeal must pay the respondent's costs.
This is because the unsuccessful application brings the appeal process to an end and the respondent is undoubtedly the successful party.

8 For the same reason, an appellant who secures permission to appeal but loses the appeal must pay the respondent's costs.7 The disposition of the appeal ends the appeal process and the respondent is the successful party.8 Costs of a successful permission-to-appeal application are, in effect, in the cause.
Time period within which to apply for costs in an amount other than default costs In Oslanski v.
Oslanski, 2021 ABCA 68, 2021 CarswellAlta 366, Justice Wakeling considered the time period within one must apply for a costs order in an amount different from that set by the default rule.

His Lordship said: [52] Rule 14.88 does not expressly stipulate the period within which a party to an appeal may seek a costs ruling different than the default rule set out in rule 14.88(1)—the successful party is entitled to a costs award from the unsuccessful party on the same scale that applies to the order appealed from. … [63]… A party must apply for a direction under rule 14.88 within two months of the pronouncement of the decision unless the party adverse in interest to the applicant agrees to a reasonable extension of time or the applicant has a compelling reason for missing the deadline if there is no agreement.

38, the Court said: [6] As a deterrent to applications to reopen appeals, generous costs awards are made when such applications are unsuccessful: Eagle Resources Ltd. v MacDonald, 2002 ABCA 12 (CanLII) at para.
Inadequate trial costs are not an argument for increased appeal costs In Geophysical Service Incorporated v.
Falkland Oil and Gas Limited, 2020 ABCA 106, 2020 CarswellAlta 751, Geophysical sued Falkland and sought $17.6M in damages.
That action was summarily dismissed, and costs were awarded to Falkland (the successful defendant).
Geophysical's appeal was dismissed, and Falkland sought appeal costs at a higher rate than that awarded at the trial level.

One of the submissions in support of higher costs was that “the trial costs award was inadequate.” On the basis of other factors, the Court of Appeal ultimately awarded appeal costs at a slightly higher rate than those awarded in the trial court (double Column 5 increased by 45.6% for inflation, as opposed to 1.5 times Column 5 increased by 45.6%).
However, the Court of Appeal specifically stated: [5] The respondent argues in part that it should receive enhanced costs of the appeal, because the trial costs award was inadequate.
Any shortcomings in the trial costs award should have been dealt with by a direct appeal.
Revisiting trial costs after successful appeal In Dunn v.
042 0105, 2024 ABCA 103, after the Court of Appeal allowed an appeal from a trial judge’s decision, the successful Appellant asked the Court of Appeal to revisit the trial costs decision.
The Court of Appeal decided that each party should bear its own costs at the trial level.

The Court gave this summary of the law: [5] When the result at trial is reversed on appeal, the basis for the costs award at trial disappears and this Court can revisit the matter of trial costs, even if there was no error as to trial costs: MacPhail v Karasek, 2006 ABCA 354 at para 8 citing FFM Holdings Ltd v Lilydale Co-operative Limited, 2002 ABCA 113.

The presumption in r 10.29 that the party who enjoys substantial success at trial will be entitled to costs against the unsuccessful party continues to apply and successful appellants usually are also entitled to trial costs: Vallieres v Vozniak, 2014 ABCA 384 at para 6, cited in Turner v Bell Mobility, 2016 ABCA 188 at para 8.

[6] In rare circumstances, trial courts will exercise their discretion to award costs against a successful party, for example where there has been misconduct, or in significant public interest cases: Mark Orkin, The Law of Costs, 2nd Ed (Aurora: Canada Law Book, 2007 – Proview) at § 2:39 and cases cited therein, Stubicar v Calgary (City) Subdivision and Development Appeal Board, 2023 ABCA 98 at paras 50-51 (single judge).

This Court may choose not to disturb an award of costs at trial in favour of a losing party in a case involving special and peculiar problems: 321665 Alberta Ltd v Husky Oil Operations Ltd, 2013 ABCA 326 at para 5, citing Alberta Public Schools Association v Alberta (Attorney General), 1998 ABCA 238, 216 AR 249 at paras 17 and 20.
[7] This Court’s discretion to award costs must be exercised judicially. …

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.90:1 Rule 14.90 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.90. 1. “Lateness”—Important comment regarding unintended consequences In Sobeys West Inc. v. Edmonton (City), 2015 ABCA 32, 2015 CarswellAlta 93, Justice Slatter said, at paragraphs 18–19: 18 Failure to meet the deadlines in R. 14.40(2) and R. 14.41 has various consequences. Rule 14.90(1)(a)(i) contains a presumption that no costs are available for a late step. The Registry or the presiding judge may decline to set down a matter that has missed the deadline, depending on the number of matters scheduled that week and other considerations. Late filing by a respondent will not be allowed to prejudice an applicant: R. 1.5(4). Extreme cases of missed deadlines can result in appeals or applications being struck. 19 Litigants before the Court should, however, be aware that there is another meaning of “lateness” in this context. The Registry will deliver the application materials for any particular week to the presiding judge before some of these formal deadlines are reached. Documents filed after that date are “late”, in the sense that the rest of the material will already have been sent to the judge. While “last minute” filings will not be subject to the consequences mentioned in para. 18, lateness in filing may require an adjournment of the hearing into the future. Whether that is necessary depends on a number of factors, including the complexity of the application, the volume of material, the number of applications set down that week, and the other responsibilities of the presiding judge. Prudent counsel will file early, and certainly will not wait until the Monday after the weekend to file documents.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.90:2 Late filing See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.90. The appellant should have its costs here and in Queen's Bench. However, the appellant's factum and revised factum were filed late. Because of the complexity of the matter the appellant asks us to waive R. 538(4) which disallows costs for late facta. We see here no illness, accident or poverty. While the respondent may not have been prejudiced, the court is prejudiced when facta are filed late. So are litigants in other appeals; setting lists and giving fixed dates becomes impossible when facta arrive late or not at all. We decline to waive R. 538(4); there will be no costs for either of the appellant's facta. Act Computer Services Ltd. v. Miller (1990), 72 Alta. L.R. (2d) 207 at 209-10 (C.A.). 1. Careful Drafting Necessary Draft the factum carefully—it can affect costs. The appellants advanced nine grounds of appeal in a factum some 80 pages long which was notable for its breach of R. 540 of the Rules of Court. It did not set out a concise statement of facts, did not clearly specify the grounds of appeal, and did not specify in a concise fashion the arguments respecting them. It was a lengthy and rambling written argument. The judge of this court fixing the list on which this case was set for hearing called counsel into chambers when the length of the appellants' factum was drawn to her attention. Counsel for the respondent however, stated that, rather than to delay the hearing of the appeal, he would prefer to proceed with the appellants' improper factum and it was so ordered. Counsel for the appellants now contends that by taking that position counsel for the respondent precluded himself from further complaint about it. We do not agree. It is clear that he urged that the appeal proceed, despite the improper factum, because the matter was urgent. The unduly prolix factum complicated and lengthened the hearing of the appeal and must be taken in consideration in fixing costs. Canadian Superior Oil Ltd. v. Jacobson (1991), 82 Alta. L.R. (2d) 250 at 251 (C.A.). The Court of Appeal also said: If either party wishes to apply for costs before the chambers judge or on appeal, he or she is free to do so. However, in preparing their submissions in this regard counsel should keep in mind that • In the appeal book at least one affidavit contains handwritten notes apparently made by the party opposing the deponent; • The appeal book does not comply with paragraph B.6 of the Consolidated Practice Directions of the Court of Appeal; • Part III of the appellant's factum which deals with points of law does not comply with rule 540(1) of the Rules of Court. There are no references to pages in the appeal book in that part; and • The respondent's factum was filed late. Rankin v. Rankin (1992), 125 A.R. 58 at 60 (C.A.).

paragraphs.text: 14.91. Duties of a Registrar

paragraphs.text: (1) A Registrar must perform the duties required by these rules and the Court of Appeal, including, subject to any direction of the Court, (a) establishing and maintaining a court file for each appeal, (b) establishing and maintaining lists of appeals, including the Civil Appeal Hearing List, (c) receiving and filing all appeal materials, having control and custody of them, and distributing them to the judges as required, (d) attending in court as required and keeping a record of all proceedings before the Court and its judges, including (i) keeping records of particulars of the appeals heard and the judges in attendance, (ii) identifying the appearing parties and their counsel, (iii) keeping records of particulars of the appeal heard and the result of the appeal, and (iv) noting the time occupied in hearing, (e) keeping proper accounts of money and property received or dispersed, (f) settling and signing judgments and orders in accordance with these rules, and (g) at the conclusion of an appeal, returning to the court appealed from any records of that court.
